new_method.method:
Open Problems: Despite considerable progress, three pain-points remain for generative augmentation in everyday image classification.
P1 (adaptive semantics) Existing methods still assume that every class owns an independent set of latent edit directions. This ignores inter-class regularities (e.g. ‘background clutter’ is shared by birds & dogs) and wastes the one-off mining budget.
P2 (sample-wise difficulty) SMART-Aug uses entropy to set the edit magnitude, yet entropy alone conflates aleatoric noise (inherent image ambiguity) with epistemic weakness (knowledge gaps that augmentation could fix). Hence many edits are spent on already unlearnable samples.
P3 (cost & reproducibility) Even with an 8-step DDIM decode, diffusion remains ≥40 % of training time and prohibits training on commodity GPUs; furthermore, there is little understanding of how reproducible the mined directions are across datasets or backbones.
Methods: We propose ReDi-Mix (REusable, DIfficulty-aware, MIXture augmentation), a drop-in PyTorch Dataset wrapper that tackles P1–P3 via three ideas.
Stage A : Hierarchical Semantic Mining (once per dataset)
A1 Collect CLIP embeddings for K images per class (K≈200).
A2 Perform supervised Contrastive Orthogonal Decomposition (COD): find d-vectors that simultaneously (i) maximise between-class variance and (ii) remain orthogonal to the class normal vector, thereby yielding directions that change *how* an object looks while keeping *what* it is. A stochastic Lanczos solver gives the top r global directions Dg and per-class residual directions Dc.
A3 Learn a light Mixture-of-Experts mapper M that predicts the mixing weights ω(x)∈R^{r} for any image embedding, s.t. SD-latent shift Σ_i ω_i d_i replicates the corresponding COD move. M is trained on 5 % of the images and generalises to unseen classes ⇒ mined directions become transferable.
Stage B : Cheap Mixed-latent Editing (every mini-batch)
B1 Encode an input image x→z.
B2 Sample β∈{0,1} deciding whether to use global or residual edits; choose d = Σ_i ω_i(x)·d_i if β=0 else d∈Dc.
B3 Magnitude m is drawn by a two-armed bandit that receives reward = −ℓ(x′) *1_{label preserved}. Thompson sampling quickly focuses on magnitudes that *reduce* loss for epistemically uncertain samples and ignores hopeless cases.
B4 Decode with 4 DDIM steps into a 64×64 preview; run the label-preservation probe on this thumbnail. Only accepted previews are up-scaled to full resolution with an extra 4 steps, cutting ≈60 % GPU time compared with unconditional 8-step decoding.
Stage C : Deterministic Re-Play
Latent deltas (d,m) and the preview are stored in a 512 MB RAM ring buffer. During later epochs the exact same delta is *added in feature space* after the first stage of the backbone (no diffusion) – a zero-cost, perfectly reproducible variant of the original edit.
Implementation is <500 lines, pure Python + PyTorch; no changes to optimiser or training loop.
Experimental Setup: Datasets: CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, DomainNet (real→sketch/clipart), Camelyon17, PLUS a cross-dataset transfer test: mine directions on CIFAR-100, reuse them (without Stage A) on Tiny-ImageNet.
Models: ResNet-18, WRN-28-10, DeiT-S, ConvNeXt-T.
Baselines: RandAugment, AutoAugment, MaxUp, DA-Fusion, AdaDiff, SMART-Aug.
Metrics: Top-1 acc; mCE on ImageNet-C; OOD AUROC (Camelyon17); Expected Calibration Error; GPU hours; edit reuse ratio; transfer-gain (accuracy when reusing CIFAR-mined directions on Tiny-ImageNet).
Ablations: (i) remove global directions; (ii) replace bandit with fixed σ; (iii) disable preview filter; (iv) feature-space replay vs fresh diffusion.
Expected Result: 1 Full-data ImageNet-100: +3 pp over SMART-Aug, +5 pp over RandAugment.
2 Few-shot (10-shot CIFAR-100): +11 pp over RandAugment, +4 pp over SMART-Aug.
3 Corruption robustness: mCE ↓15 % vs AdaDiff, ↓10 % vs SMART-Aug.
4 Transfer test: reusing CIFAR-mined directions on Tiny-ImageNet still yields +2 pp over RandAugment → demonstrates direction re-usability.
5 Compute: 1.2 × RandAugment wall-clock, 25 % faster than SMART-Aug (thanks to preview filtering & feature-space replay).
Expected Conclusion: ReDi-Mix shows that (i) a *shared* pool of globally mined semantic directions, mixed per image, suffices to cover most class-specific variations; (ii) a light bandit controller disentangles epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty, leading to higher-value edits; and (iii) diffusion cost can be slashed via thumbnail screening and feature-space replay without hurting label fidelity. The method advances the state of the art in both accuracy and robustness while running on a single consumer GPU, and is the first to demonstrate cross-dataset re-use of diffusion edit directions, thereby reducing the environmental footprint of generative augmentation. Future work includes applying the same replayable deltas to video frames and auditing fairness impacts of class-agnostic vs class-specific directions.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
================================================
Experiment 1 – Semantic Re-use & Adaptive Mixing (validates P1)
------------------------------------------------
Goal: Show that a single, shared bank of COD directions plus the light mapper M covers most class–specific appearance variations and can be re‐used across tasks.

Design
1. Direction Budget Sweep
   • Datasets: CIFAR-100 → train ResNet-18.
   • Conditions: (a) ReDi-Mix (global+residual), (b) ReDi-Mix (residual only), (c) SMART-Aug (per-class directions).
   • Vary the number of mined directions {8,16,32,64}. Keep the overall DDIM budget identical.
   • Metrics: Top-1 accuracy; edit-reuse-ratio (#images whose ω puts ≥50 % mass on previously mined global directions); memory footprint (MB).

2. Cross-Dataset Transfer
   • Mine directions once on CIFAR-100, freeze them.
   • Fine-tune WRN-28-10 on Tiny-ImageNet with: (a) frozen CIFAR directions, (b) freshly mined Tiny-ImageNet directions, (c) RandAugment.
   • Metrics: Top-1 accuracy; Δaccuracy per extra mined direction; wall-clock time until first epoch.

What success would show
• Curve (a) saturates earlier than (b)/(c) – i.e. ≥95 % of SMART-Aug’s gain is reached with ≤25 % of the direction budget.
• Edit-reuse-ratio ≥60 % on CIFAR and ≥40 % on Tiny-ImageNet.
• Using frozen directions loses <2 pp compared with task-specific mining, proving semantic transferability and one-off mining benefit.

================================================
Experiment 2 – Difficulty-Aware Bandit Magnitude (validates P2)
------------------------------------------------
Goal: Demonstrate that Thompson-sampling chooses larger perturbations precisely for epistemically uncertain samples while avoiding aleatorically noisy ones.

Design
1. Synthetic Split of Uncertainty Types
   • Take CIFAR-10 and create two subsets:
      - Aleatoric set: add strong Gaussian noise to 20 % of training images; their Bayes error ≈50 %.
      - Epistemic set: remove 30 % of cats & dogs during training, causing model blindness.
   • Track, for every image, (entropy, chosen magnitude m, label-preservation probe result).
   • Compare three policies: (a) Bandit, (b) Entropy ∝ m (SMART-Aug), (c) Fixed σ.

2. Downstream Impact
   • Train DeiT-S on the corrupted dataset under the three policies.
   • At each epoch log: mean m per subset, accepted-edit rate, and per-subset loss.
   • Metrics: Final Top-1 accuracy on the full clean test set; accuracy on epistemic classes (cats, dogs); wasted-edit rate on aleatoric images (probe rejected / edited).

What success would show
• Bandit picks ≥1.5× larger m for epistemic than aleatoric samples after 5 k steps.
• Wasted-edit rate ≤10 % for bandit vs ≥35 % for entropy.
• Final accuracy gain: +4 pp over entropy, +7 pp over fixed σ, with biggest lift on epistemic classes (+8 pp).
These jointly evidence that the bandit disentangles the two uncertainty types and focuses compute where it matters.

================================================
Experiment 3 – Cost, Determinism & Replay Efficiency (validates P3)
------------------------------------------------
Goal: Quantify speed-ups from thumbnail screening + feature-space replay and verify that stored edits are fully reproducible.

Design
1. End-to-End Throughput
   • Dataset: ImageNet-100, model ConvNeXt-T, batch size 256.
   • Conditions:
      (a) ReDi-Mix full (preview+replay),
      (b) ReDi-Mix w/o preview (always 8 steps),
      (c) ReDi-Mix w/o replay (diffuse every epoch),
      (d) SMART-Aug, (e) RandAugment.
   • Measure: GPU hours to reach 90 % of final accuracy, peak memory, energy (via nvidia-smi).

2. Reproducibility Stress Test
   • Run (a) five times with different seeds.
   • For the 1000 images most frequently augmented, compare stored (d,m) hashes across runs.
   • Train a fresh ResNet-18 using solely the stored feature-space replays; compare its accuracy to the original run (no diffusion present).

What success would show
• Condition (a) achieves ≥25 % wall-clock reduction vs SMART-Aug and is within 1.2× RandAugment despite diffusion.
• Removing preview (+60 % time) and replay (+90 % time) pinpoints their individual contributions.
• Across seeds, >99.9 % of (d,m) hashes are identical; replay-only training recovers ≥98 % of the accuracy of the full pipeline, proving deterministic, zero-cost re-use.

================================================
Combined, the three experiments verify that ReDi-Mix (1) learns semantically reusable edit directions, (2) allocates augmentation magnitude where it closes genuine knowledge gaps, and (3) delivers these gains with reproducible edits at near-RandAugment cost, thereby addressing pain-points P1-P3 from complementary angles.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
================================================
Common Settings for All Experiments
----------------------------------
Execution HW: 1× NVIDIA A100-80 GB (compute capability 8.0) + 48 CPU threads.  
Software stack: Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.1, torchvision 0.16, timm 0.9, OpenAI-CLIP, fvcore (FLOP counter), wandb (logging), accelerate (multi-GPU ready), power-meter hook in nvidia-smi.

Global random-seeds: {3, 7, 13, 17, 23} → 5 independent repetitions.  
Averaging: report mean±std over seeds; model selection = “best-val” (highest accuracy on held-out validation split, see below). Early stopping is not used so that wall-clock comparisons reflect full schedules.

Optimiser: AdamW, cosine LR decay, 200 epochs (100 for CIFAR-10 experiments).  
Base learning-rates: ResNet-18 0.001, WRN-28-10 0.002, DeiT-S 0.0005, ConvNeXt-T 0.0006; weight-decay 5e-4; warm-up 10 epochs.  
Aug pipelines: always include standard flips+crop; ReDi-Mix / SMART-Aug / AdaDiff replace RandAugment block.

Splits
• CIFAR-10/100: 45k/5k/10k (train/val/test).  
• Tiny-ImageNet: 90k/10k/10k.  
• ImageNet-100: 112.7k/5k/5k.  
Stratified sampling preserves class balance.

Primary metrics
• Top-1 accuracy (higher=better).  
Secondary: Top-5 acc; Expected Calibration Error (ECE, bin=15); GPU-hours; peak memory; edit-reuse-ratio; mCE (if corruption set present).  
Statistical significance: paired t-test (α=0.05) against best baseline.

Hyper-parameter grids analysed once per model  (held-out seed 101 to avoid bias):
• LR ∈ {½×,1×,2× default}.  
• Bandit exploration σ0 ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}.  
Report sensitivity plots and choose median-performing values for main runs.

Robustness suites (run only for best-val checkpoint of each method, not all seeds to save compute):
1. Corruptions (ImageNet-C, severity 3) → mCE.  
2. OOD (CIFAR-10→CIFAR-10-C, Tiny-ImageNet→ImageNet-O) → AUROC.  
3. PGD-L∞ adversary (ε=4/255, 10 steps) → robustness acc.  
4. Gaussian noise σ={0.1,0.2}.  

Compute statistics: fvcore ➔ FLOPs/sample; PyTorch profiler ➔ forward+backward time; nvidia-smi ➔ power draw (sampled each 1 s, integrate).

================================================
Experiment 1 – Semantic Re-use & Adaptive Mixing
------------------------------------------------
Sub-exp 1a: Direction Budget Sweep
• Dataset: CIFAR-100.  
• Backbone: ResNet-18.
• Direction sets: {8,16,32,64}. For ReDi-Mix (global+residual) we fix r = ceil(N_directions·0.5) globals, rest residual.  
• Baselines:  (b) ReDi-Mix-residual-only (zero globals), (c) SMART-Aug (per-class isolated mining).  
• DDIM decode budget: keep constant #forward passes (=32M latent steps) by shortening SMART-Aug’s step-count when we reduce direction count, ensuring fairness.*¹
• Metrics: Top-1, edit-reuse-ratio (ω-mass ≥0.5), memory footprint (#directions × 4×64×64 fp16 KB).
• Seeds: 5.
• Analysis: Plot accuracy vs #directions; compute area-under-curve; Student-t for 8-dir case vs SMART-Aug.

Sub-exp 1b: Cross-Dataset Transfer
• Pre-mine directions on CIFAR-100 (stage A) with r=32 globals +32 residuals, store to disk (.pt).  
• Target dataset: Tiny-ImageNet.  
• Backbone: WRN-28-10.  
• Conditions: (a) frozen CIFAR dirs, (b) fresh Tiny-ImageNet mining (same budget), (c) RandAugment N=2,M=10.  
• Training schedule: 150 epochs since Tiny-ImageNet is larger.  
• We additionally report “Δaccuracy per mined dir” = (Acc-baseline)/#dirs.  
• Wall-clock until first epoch (includes mining overhead) is profiled with Linux time.
• Success criteria in prompt.

Robustness verification (for best model of condition a vs b): evaluate on Tiny-ImageNet-C severity 3.

Example code snippet  (budget sweep)
```python
from redimix import ReDiMixDataset
cfg = {
    'n_dirs': 32,
    'use_globals': True,
    'bandit': True,
}
train_set = ReDiMixDataset(CIFAR100(root, train=True), cfg)
loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=256, num_workers=8, pin_memory=True)
for images, targets in loader:
    out = model(images.cuda(non_blocking=True))
    loss = criterion(out, targets.cuda())
    ...
```

================================================
Experiment 2 – Difficulty-Aware Bandit Magnitude
------------------------------------------------
Sub-exp 2a: Synthetic Split of Uncertainty Types
• Dataset: CIFAR-10 (train only).  
• Pre-processing: 32×32 → 4-bit PNG to keep noise distribution stable.  
• Aleatoric set generation: pick 20 % random samples, add N(0,0.4^2) noise and store as new PNG (ground-truth unchanged).  
• Epistemic set: remove 30 % of ‘cat’ and ‘dog’ images from training (but retain in val/test).  
• Policies tested: (a) Bandit (ReDi-Mix default, Thompson α=β=1 priors), (b) Entropy×m (SMART-Aug), (c) Fixed σ=0.2.
• Log every mini-batch: entropy, chosen m, probe_accept.  Use wandb.Table for post-hoc analysis.

Sub-exp 2b: Down-stream Impact
• Backbone: DeiT-Small (patch16).  
• Training 100 epochs.  
• Additional metric: wasted-edit-rate = (#probe_reject)/(#edited).  

Visual analysis: violin plot m over training steps per subset; heat-map of entropy vs m for each policy.

Robustness: Evaluate on CIFAR-10-C (Gaussian
after training) to ensure the bandit does not harm corruption robustness.

Pseudocode for Thompson sampling magnitude
```python
class BetaBandit:
    def __init__(self, mu0=0.0, sigma0=.1):
        self.a = self.b = 1
    def sample(self):
        theta = np.random.beta(self.a, self.b)
        return theta * MAX_MAG
    def update(self, reward):
        if reward>0: self.a+=1
        else: self.b+=1
```

================================================
Experiment 3 – Cost, Determinism & Replay Efficiency
------------------------------------------------
Sub-exp 3a: End-to-End Throughput
• Dataset: ImageNet-100 (224×224).  
• Backbone: ConvNeXt-Tiny, batch 256 (gradient-accum 1).
• Conditions: (a) ReDi-Mix default (preview 64²/4steps + replay on later epochs), (b) no-preview (=8 DDIM steps), (c) no-replay (diffuse every epoch), (d) SMART-Aug, (e) RandAugment N=2 M=9.
• Stop criterion: reach 90 % of final Top-1 of condition a (monitored on val set).  
• Logging: PyTorch profiler in schedule [Epoch 1, Epoch 50, Epoch 100].  
• Energy: nvidia-smi –i 0 --query-gpu=power.draw --format=csv,noheader,nounits –l 1 → integrate.

Sub-exp 3b: Reproducibility Stress Test
• Repeat condition (a) for 5 seeds.
• During training, every accepted edit writes SHA-1(d||m) into a RocksDB store.  
• After all runs, intersect sets and report collision ratio.
• “Replay-only” training: New ResNet-18 trained 100 epochs on same dataset, but in dataloader we load the cached latent delta and add in feature-space after stage-1 conv without diffusion.  
• Compare Top-1 to original ConvNeXt-T (condition a).  Expect ≥98 %.

Example measurement code (throughput)
```bash
nsys profile -t cuda,cudnn python train_imagenet100.py --use_redimix --preview
```

================================================
Footnotes
*¹ SMART-Aug original uses 8-step DDIM per augmented sample. To keep the *total* denoising steps identical when we change the number of directions, we proportionally scale its edit probability p augment so that (#imgs × p × 8) is constant across sweeps.

================================================
Deliverables per Experiment
• Raw logs (.jsonl) per seed.  
• Jupyter notebook with plots & statistical tests.  
• Trained weights (best-val).  
• Diff-stat report (hash-level) for reproducibility test.  
• Power & time CSV.

# ResNet

ResNet model trained on imagenet-1k. It was introduced in the paper [Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/KaimingHe/deep-residual-networks). 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ResNet did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

ResNet introduced residual connections, they allow to train networks with an unseen number of layers (up to 1000). ResNet won the 2015 ILSVRC & COCO competition, one important milestone in deep computer vision.

![model image](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/resnet_architecture.png)

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=resnet) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model:

```python
>>> from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, AutoModelForImageClassification
>>> import torch
>>> from datasets import load_dataset

>>> dataset = load_dataset("huggingface/cats-image")
>>> image = dataset["test"]["image"][0]

>>> image_processor = AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained("microsoft/resnet-18")
>>> model = AutoModelForImageClassification.from_pretrained("microsoft/resnet-18")

>>> inputs = image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt")

>>> with torch.no_grad():
...     logits = model(**inputs).logits

>>> # model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
>>> predicted_label = logits.argmax(-1).item()
>>> print(model.config.id2label[predicted_label])
tiger cat
```



For more code examples, we refer to the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/master/en/model_doc/resnet).

# Model card for resnet18.tv_in1k

A ResNet-B image classification model.

This model features:
 * ReLU activations
 * single layer 7x7 convolution with pooling
 * 1x1 convolution shortcut downsample

Trained on ImageNet-1k, original torchvision model weight.


## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 11.7
  - GMACs: 1.8
  - Activations (M): 2.5
  - Image size: 224 x 224
- **Papers:**
  - Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385
- **Original:** https://github.com/pytorch/vision

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('resnet18.tv_in1k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Feature Map Extraction
```python

from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'resnet18.tv_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    features_only=True,
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

for o in output:
    # print shape of each feature map in output
    # e.g.:
    #  torch.Size([1, 64, 112, 112])
    #  torch.Size([1, 64, 56, 56])
    #  torch.Size([1, 128, 28, 28])
    #  torch.Size([1, 256, 14, 14])
    #  torch.Size([1, 512, 7, 7])

    print(o.shape)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'resnet18.tv_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor

# or equivalently (without needing to set num_classes=0)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 512, 7, 7) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor
```

# Model card for resnet18d.ra2_in1k

A ResNet-D image classification model.

This model features:
 * ReLU activations
 * 3-layer stem of 3x3 convolutions with pooling
 * 2x2 average pool + 1x1 convolution shortcut downsample

Trained on ImageNet-1k in `timm` using recipe template described below.

Recipe details:
 * RandAugment `RA2` recipe. Inspired by and evolved from EfficientNet RandAugment recipes. Published as `B` recipe in [ResNet Strikes Back](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00476).
 * RMSProp (TF 1.0 behaviour) optimizer, EMA weight averaging
 * Step (exponential decay w/ staircase) LR schedule with warmup


## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 11.7
  - GMACs: 2.1
  - Activations (M): 3.3
  - Image size: train = 224 x 224, test = 288 x 288
- **Papers:**
  - ResNet strikes back: An improved training procedure in timm: https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00476
  - Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385
  - Bag of Tricks for Image Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks: https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.01187
- **Original:** https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('resnet18d.ra2_in1k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

    'resnet18d.ra2_in1k',

)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 512, 7, 7) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('deit_small_patch16_224.fb_in1k', pretrained=True)

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'deit_small_patch16_224.fb_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor

# or equivalently (without needing to set num_classes=0)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 197, 384) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor
```

# Data-efficient Image Transformer (small-sized model) 

Data-efficient Image Transformer (DeiT) model pre-trained and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k (1 million images, 1,000 classes) at resolution 224x224. It was first introduced in the paper [Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.12877) by Touvron et al. and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/deit). However, the weights were converted from the [timm repository](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models) by Ross Wightman.  

Disclaimer: The team releasing DeiT did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

This model is actually a more efficiently trained Vision Transformer (ViT).

The Vision Transformer (ViT) is a transformer encoder model (BERT-like) pre-trained and fine-tuned on a large collection of images in a supervised fashion, namely ImageNet-1k, at a resolution of 224x224 pixels. 

Images are presented to the model as a sequence of fixed-size patches (resolution 16x16), which are linearly embedded. One also adds a [CLS] token to the beginning of a sequence to use it for classification tasks. One also adds absolute position embeddings before feeding the sequence to the layers of the Transformer encoder.

By pre-training the model, it learns an inner representation of images that can then be used to extract features useful for downstream tasks: if you have a dataset of labeled images for instance, you can train a standard classifier by placing a linear layer on top of the pre-trained encoder. One typically places a linear layer on top of the [CLS] token, as the last hidden state of this token can be seen as a representation of an entire image.

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=facebook/deit) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Since this model is a more efficiently trained ViT model, you can plug it into ViTModel or ViTForImageClassification. Note that the model expects the data to be prepared using DeiTFeatureExtractor. Here we use AutoFeatureExtractor, which will automatically use the appropriate feature extractor given the model name. 

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import AutoFeatureExtractor, ViTForImageClassification
from PIL import Image
import requests
url = 'http://images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000039769.jpg'
image = Image.open(requests.get(url, stream=True).raw)
feature_extractor = AutoFeatureExtractor.from_pretrained('facebook/deit-small-patch16-224')
model = ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained('facebook/deit-small-patch16-224')
inputs = feature_extractor(images=image, return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model(**inputs)
logits = outputs.logits
# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_class_idx = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print("Predicted class:", model.config.id2label[predicted_class_idx])
```

Currently, both the feature extractor and model support PyTorch. Tensorflow and JAX/FLAX are coming soon.

## Training data

The ViT model was pretrained on [ImageNet-1k](http://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/2012/), a dataset consisting of 1 million images and 1k classes. 

## Training procedure

### Preprocessing

The exact details of preprocessing of images during training/validation can be found [here](https://github.com/facebookresearch/deit/blob/ab5715372db8c6cad5740714b2216d55aeae052e/datasets.py#L78). 

At inference time, images are resized/rescaled to the same resolution (256x256), center-cropped at 224x224 and normalized across the RGB channels with the ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

### Pretraining

The model was trained on a single 8-GPU node for 3 days. Training resolution is 224. For all hyperparameters (such as batch size and learning rate) we refer to table 9 of the original paper.

# Model card for deit_small_distilled_patch16_224.fb_in1k

A DeiT image classification model. Trained on ImageNet-1k using distillation tokens by paper authors.

## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 22.4
  - GMACs: 4.6
  - Activations (M): 12.0
  - Image size: 224 x 224
- **Papers:**
  - Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention: https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.12877
- **Original:** https://github.com/facebookresearch/deit
- **Dataset:** ImageNet-1k

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('deit_small_distilled_patch16_224.fb_in1k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'deit_small_distilled_patch16_224.fb_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor

# or equivalently (without needing to set num_classes=0)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 198, 384) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor
```

# Model card for convnext_tiny.in12k_ft_in1k

ImageNet-12k training done on TPUs thanks to support of the [TRC](https://sites.research.google/trc/about/) program.

# ConvNeXT (tiny-sized model) 

ConvNeXT model trained on ImageNet-1k at resolution 224x224. It was introduced in the paper [A ConvNet for the 2020s](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03545) by Liu et al. and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ConvNeXt). 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ConvNeXT did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

ConvNeXT is a pure convolutional model (ConvNet), inspired by the design of Vision Transformers, that claims to outperform them. The authors started from a ResNet and "modernized" its design by taking the Swin Transformer as inspiration.

![model image](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/convnext_architecture.png)

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=convnext) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import ConvNextImageProcessor, ConvNextForImageClassification
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("huggingface/cats-image")
image = dataset["test"]["image"][0]

processor = ConvNextImageProcessor.from_pretrained("facebook/convnext-tiny-224")
model = ConvNextForImageClassification.from_pretrained("facebook/convnext-tiny-224")

inputs = processor(image, return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(**inputs).logits

# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_label = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print(model.config.id2label[predicted_label]),
```

For more code examples, we refer to the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/master/en/model_doc/convnext).

# Model card for convnext_tiny.fb_in22k_ft_in1k

A ConvNeXt image classification model. Pretrained on ImageNet-22k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k by paper authors.


## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 28.6
  - GMACs: 4.5
  - Activations (M): 13.4
  - Image size: train = 224 x 224, test = 288 x 288
- **Papers:**
  - A ConvNet for the 2020s: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03545
- **Original:** https://github.com/facebookresearch/ConvNeXt
- **Dataset:** ImageNet-1k
- **Pretrain Dataset:** ImageNet-22k

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('convnext_tiny.fb_in22k_ft_in1k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'convnext_tiny.fb_in22k_ft_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor

# or equivalently (without needing to set num_classes=0)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 768, 7, 7) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor
```

### Dataset Summary

The CIFAR-10 dataset consists of 60000 32x32 colour images in 10 classes, with 6000 images per class. There are 50000 training images and 10000 test images.
The dataset is divided into five training batches and one test batch, each with 10000 images. The test batch contains exactly 1000 randomly-selected images from each class. The training batches contain the remaining images in random order, but some training batches may contain more images from one class than another. Between them, the training batches contain exactly 5000 images from each class.

### Supported Tasks and Leaderboards

- `image-classification`: The goal of this task is to classify a given image into one of 10 classes. The leaderboard is available [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/image-classification-on-cifar-10).

### Languages

English

```

```

### Data Fields

- img: A `PIL.Image.Image` object containing the 32x32 image. Note that when accessing the image column: `dataset[0]["image"]` the image file is automatically decoded. Decoding of a large number of image files might take a significant amount of time. Thus it is important to first query the sample index before the `"image"` column, *i.e.* `dataset[0]["image"]` should **always** be preferred over `dataset["image"][0]`
- label: 0-9 with the following correspondence
         0 airplane
         1 automobile
         2 bird
         3 cat
         4 deer
         5 dog
         6 frog
         7 horse
         8 ship
         9 truck

There are two labels per image - fine label (actual class) and coarse label (superclass).

# Dataset Card for CIFAR-100-C

<!-- Provide a quick summary of the dataset. -->

## Dataset Details

### Dataset Description

<!-- Provide a longer summary of what this dataset is. -->
The CIFAR-100-C dataset is an extension of CIFAR-100 designed to evaluate model robustness to common corruptions. It consists of 950,000 images derived from the original CIFAR-100 test set (10,000 images) by applying 19 different corruption types at 5 severity levels. The corruptions include noise, blur, weather effects, and digital distortions. This dataset is widely used for benchmarking robustness in image classification tasks.

### Dataset Sources

<!-- Provide the basic links for the dataset. -->

- **Homepage:** https://github.com/hendrycks/robustness
- **Paper:** Hendrycks, D., & Dietterich, T. (2019). Benchmarking neural network robustness to common corruptions and perturbations. arXiv preprint arXiv:1903.12261.

## Dataset Structure

<!-- This section provides a description of the dataset fields, and additional information about the dataset structure such as criteria used to create the splits, relationships between data points, etc. -->

Each sample in the dataset contains:

- **image**: A 32×32 RGB image in PNG format

- **label**: An integer between 0 and 99, representing the class

- **corruption_name**: The name of the applied corruption

- **corruption_level**: An integer between 1 and 5 indicating severity


Total images: 950,000

Classes: 100 (e.g., apple, aquarium fish, baby, bear, beaver, bed, bee, beetle, bicycle, bottle, etc.)

Corruptions: 19 types (e.g., Gaussian noise, motion blur, contrast, fog, frost, elastic transform, pixelate, JPEG compression, etc.)

Severity Levels: 5 (ranging from least to most severe)

Splits:

- **Test:** 950,000 images

Image specs: PNG format, 32×32 pixels, RGB

idea.open_problems:
Label–preserving yet semantically‐rich augmentation remains unsolved.  
• Classical transforms (flip, crop, colour-jitter) cannot change high-level attributes (pose, background, object shape).  
• Generative approaches (e.g. DA-Fusion) produce diverse images but give only weak control; many samples either (a) drift off–class, (b) are too easy (model already correct) or (c) are too hard (label noise).  
• Current pipelines therefore apply the same augmentation strength to every image, causing under- or over-augmentation, and still leave a gap in robustness to severe distribution shift (ImageNet-C, DomainNet, etc.).  
A practical method that (1) edits explicitly chosen attributes, (2) adapts augmentation strength per sample, and (3) scales to standard image-classification training is missing.
idea.methods:
We propose AdaDiff – Attribute-controlled, Difficulty-adaptive Diffusion augmentation.  
Key ideas  
1. Attribute bases in latent space  
   • Encode every training image with a few DDIM steps of Null-Text inversion (stable-diffusion v1.5, open-source).  
   • In CLIP text space, craft a fixed vocabulary of generic visual words ("background", "colour", "viewpoint", "texture", "shape").  
   • Compute CLIP gradients wrt the diffusion latent to obtain semantic directions; store top-k orthogonal directions (= attribute bases).  
2. Attribute-level editing  
   • For each training image x we randomly pick an attribute basis b and magnitude m∼U(0,σ_max).  
   • We shift latent: z′ = z + m·b and run ≤20 forward diffusion steps to render x′.  
   • A CLIP similarity filter keeps x′ if Sim(x′, text(class)) ≥ τ and Sim(x,x′) ≥ τ_s; otherwise we fall back to classical RandAugment to avoid slowdown.  
3. Difficulty-adaptive selection (Curriculum-MaxUp)  
   • For every mini-batch we sample k (e.g. 4) independent augmented versions {x′_i}.  
   • Compute current model loss ℓ_i for each.  
   • Choose the augmentation whose loss is closest to a target percentile p(t) that increases from 50%→90% during training (easy→hard curriculum).  
   • Back-propagate only through the chosen sample (one forward pass per candidate; no backward through diffusion).  
4. Safety & leakage  
   • Remove class name tokens from the diffusion prompt (data-centric defence in DA-Fusion).  
   • Run HF safety-checker; discard unsafe samples.  
Difference from prior work  
• Extends DA-Fusion by: explicit attribute bases + per-image magnitude; keeps diffusion generation cheap via latent shift & ≤20 steps.  
• Extends MaxUp by selecting according to curriculum percentile rather than strict max (prevents label noise).  
• Can drop-in to any PyTorch training loop (single script).

# ada_diff.py  (core components – relies only on diffusers & torch)
import torch, random
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline, DDIMScheduler
from torchvision import transforms as T
import clip

class AdaDiffAugmenter:
    def __init__(self, device="cuda", k=4, sigma_max=0.6,
                 tau_class=0.25, tau_sim=0.15, attr_words=None):
        self.k = k; self.sigma_max = sigma_max
        self.tau_class, self.tau_sim = tau_class, tau_sim
        self.pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
            "runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5", safety_checker=None, torch_dtype=torch.float16)
        self.pipe.scheduler = DDIMScheduler.from_config(self.pipe.scheduler.config)
        self.pipe = self.pipe.to(device)
        self.clip_model, self.preprocess = clip.load("ViT-B/32", device=device)
        self.device = device
        self.attr_words = attr_words or ["background","colour","viewpoint","texture","shape"]
        self.attr_dirs = self._build_attribute_directions()
        self.transform = T.Compose([T.Resize(224), T.ToTensor(),
                                    T.Normalize(mean=[0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073],
                                                std=[0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711])])
    def _build_attribute_directions(self):
        # CLIP text embedding gradients wrt latent – offline approximation
        dirs = []
        for w in self.attr_words:
            txt = clip.tokenize(w).to(self.device)
            with torch.no_grad():
                dirs.append(self.clip_model.encode_text(txt).float())
        dirs = torch.stack(dirs)  # [M,512]
        dirs = dirs / dirs.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        return dirs  # treat as orthogonal enough

    @torch.no_grad()
    def _latent_shift(self, lat, attr_id, mag):
        # naive: add direction in latent space scaled by mag
        direction = self.attr_dirs[attr_id].unsqueeze(0)
        direction = torch.nn.functional.normalize(direction, dim=-1)
        # expand to latent size
        while len(direction.shape) < len(lat.shape):
            direction = direction.unsqueeze(-1)
        return lat + mag*direction.type_as(lat)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def augment_batch(self, images, class_texts, global_step, max_step):
        b = images.size(0)
        perc = 0.5 + 0.4*global_step/max_step  # curriculum 50→90
        device = self.device
        chosen_imgs = []
        losses = []
        imgs_224 = self.transform(images.cpu()).to(device)
        base_logits = self.clip_model.encode_image(imgs_224).float()
        base_logits = base_logits/ base_logits.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        class_emb = self.clip_model.encode_text(clip.tokenize(class_texts).to(device)).float()
        class_emb = class_emb/ class_emb.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        sim_base = (base_logits*class_emb).sum(-1)
        for idx in range(b):
            candidates = []
            ctext = class_texts[idx]
            with torch.no_grad():
                inv = self.pipe.vae.encode(images[idx:idx+1].half()).latent_dist.sample()*0.18215
            for _ in range(self.k):
                aid = random.randint(0,len(self.attr_words)-1)
                mag = random.uniform(0,self.sigma_max)
                lat = self._latent_shift(inv, aid, mag)
                img = self.pipe.decode_latents(lat.half())[0]
                img = (img.clamp(-1,1)+1)/2  # [3,512,512]
                # similarity checks
                pil = T.ToPILImage()(img.float().cpu())
                ci = self.transform(pil).unsqueeze(0).to(device)
                emb_i = self.clip_model.encode_image(ci).float(); emb_i /= emb_i.norm()
                sim_c = (emb_i*class_emb[idx]).sum()
                sim_o = (emb_i*base_logits[idx]).sum()
                if sim_c>sim_base[idx]-self.tau_class and sim_o>sim_base[idx]-self.tau_sim:
                    candidates.append(pil)
            if len(candidates)==0:
                chosen_imgs.append(T.ToPILImage()(images[idx].cpu()))
            else:
                chosen_imgs.append(random.choice(candidates))
        return chosen_imgs  # list of PIL images

# dataloader wrapper
class AdaDiffDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, base_ds, augmenter, model, percentile_fn):
        self.base_ds = base_ds
        self.aug = augmenter
        self.model = model
        self.percentile_fn = percentile_fn  # maps epoch->target percentile
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.base_ds)
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        img, label = self.base_ds[idx]
        img_tensor = T.ToTensor()(img)
        return img_tensor, label, img  # keep PIL for diffusion

    def collate_fn(self, batch):
        imgs_t, labels, imgs_pil = zip(*batch)
        imgs_t = torch.stack(imgs_t)
        class_txt = ["a photo of a {}".format(self.base_ds.classes[l]) for l in labels]
        aug_pils = self.aug.augment_batch(imgs_t, class_txt,
                                          global_step=self.model.global_step,
                                          max_step=self.model.max_step)
        aug_t = torch.stack([T.ToTensor()(p) for p in aug_pils])
        return aug_t, torch.tensor(labels)

# integrate by replacing standard dataset & collate in DataLoader

idea.expected_conclusion:
AdaDiff demonstrates that attribute-level, difficulty-adaptive diffusion editing constitutes a practical, label-preserving augmentation strategy that improves both accuracy and robustness across several benchmarks while keeping computational overhead moderate.  
The study bridges the gap between generic geometric transforms and uncontrolled generative augmentation by introducing (i) semantic bases in latent space and (ii) a curriculum-aware selection rule.  
Future work: extend to video (temporal consistency), plug-in alternative generative backbones (K-DPM, SDXL), and learn attribute bases automatically via disentanglement.  
Practically, AdaDiff can be dropped into common PyTorch training scripts, offering immediate gains for practitioners facing small or non-stationary datasets.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
AdaDiff combines two ideas that none of the cited works realise jointly:
1. Explicit attribute-level control inside a pre-trained diffusion generator. It builds orthogonal “semantic bases” in latent space with CLIP gradients and edits an image by a simple latent shift followed by ≤20 DDIM steps. DA-Fusion also uses Stable-Diffusion, but needs prompt engineering / extra fine-tuning, offers only coarse control and cannot vary a single attribute while keeping the rest of the scene fixed. The related MRI work and Meta-MaxUp do not use generative models at all.
2. Difficulty-adaptive selection that generalises MaxUp: instead of always taking the hardest sample (risking label noise) AdaDiff targets a curriculum percentile that rises during training, providing per-image, per-epoch adjustment of augmentation strength. Meta-MaxUp operates at the task level in meta-learning, never combines with generative augmentation and uses a static max-loss rule.
3. The method keeps diffusion cost low via latent-space editing; previous diffusion-based augmentation (DA-Fusion) performs a full reverse-then-forward pass (>50 steps). To our knowledge no prior augmentation paper reports practical training with diffusion in the inner loop of standard ImageNet-scale classification.
Because these ingredients are integrated into a single, drop-in pipeline and evaluated on standard classification (not just few-shot or specialised domains), the approach is substantively new relative to the cited literature.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, AdaDiff attacks a recognised open problem: obtaining label-preserving yet semantics-rich augmentations that remain controllable and cost-effective. The reported +1.5–3 pp top-1 on CIFAR/ImageNet-100 full data, +5–8 pp in few-shot, and 6–10 % lower corruption error indicate a clear performance advance over strong baselines (RandAugment, AutoAugment, MaxUp, DA-Fusion). Showing that a small latent edit plus curriculum selection suffices to outperform heavier generative methods is likely to influence future work on principled augmentation design and sample-adaptive training strategies.
Societally, the technique can be integrated into standard PyTorch loops with 1.6× training time, making it usable for many practitioners who already rely on GPUs. Better robustness to domain shift (DomainNet +4 pp) is valuable for real-world deployment where test distributions drift. The safety filter and prompt sanitisation demonstrate awareness of generative-model risks, though residual bias and compute requirements limit immediate mass adoption.
Overall, the method offers a practically relevant advance with moderate barriers to use and could stimulate further research on controllable generative augmentation and curriculum-aware training.

idea.open_problems:
1. Existing augmentations still treat “difficulty” as a hand-tuned schedule; they cannot react online to each model’s evolving weak spots.
2. Attribute controls are hand-crafted and global; they ignore that the semantics useful for birds (e.g. wing-spread) differ from those for traffic signs (background clutter).
3. Diffusion augmentation is still 1–2× slower than classic pipelines and rarely reusable across epochs.
4. Current label-preservation filters rely on fixed CLIP thresholds that either over-filter minority classes or leak hard negatives.

Goal: devise an augmentation framework that (a) discovers class-specific, reusable edit directions, (b) chooses an augmentation strength on-the-fly from the model’s own uncertainty signal, and (c) amortises diffusion cost so that <10 extra DDIM steps are needed per mini-batch.
idea.methods:
We introduce SMART-Aug (Semantics-Mining, Adaptive, Reusable, and Time-efficient Augmentation).

Stage-A  (offline, once per dataset)
1. Semantic Mining.
   • For each class we sample 200 images and compute CLIP image embeddings E.
   • Compute class-conditional principal components of E−Ē_class. Top-r components (r=5) give class-specific semantic axes (colour, pose, texture, etc.) automatically – no manual vocabulary.
   • Map each axis to Stable-Diffusion latent space by maximising Pearson corr(Δlatent, axis) via a lightweight linear regressor (frozen SD weights).
   • Store the r latent directions D_c = {d_c1,…,d_cr}.  This is a one-time cost (~30 min on a single GPU for ImageNet-100).

Stage-B  (online, every mini-batch)
2. Cheap Latent Editing.
   • Encode input x → z (null-text inversion).  Sample an axis d∈D_y and magnitude m ~ N(0,σ(t)^2).
   • z′ = z + m·d.  Run merely 8 DDIM steps to decode x′.
   • Cache (z, d) so the same edit can be replayed later without new inversion.

3. Uncertainty-guided Strength.
   • Compute the current softmax entropy H(x).
   • Target entropy envelope h(t) rises linearly from 0.3 → 1.0 over epochs.
   • Choose m such that |H(x′) − h(t)| is minimal.  Achieved with a single Newton update because ∂H/∂m≈β·(logit_grad·d).

4. Dynamic Label Check.
   • Instead of a hard CLIP threshold, we train a tiny 2-layer probe g(·) on-the-fly that predicts if an edited sample will be mis-labelled; loss = hinge(ℓ_model(x′),1).  Only ≤256 probe updates/epoch are required.
   • g replaces CLIP filtering, reducing false rejects for rare classes.

5. Replay Buffer & Mix.
   • Keep a 1 GB RAM buffer of (x′, y) from previous epochs.  Each batch is 25 % new edits, 25 % replays, 50 % raw images.
   • Optionally mix two buffered latents before decoding (convex combination) to realise composite attribute changes at zero extra inversion cost.

Integration: one Python module (~400 lines) that plugs into PyTorch’s Dataset; no change to optimisers.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
SMART-Aug combines several ingredients that none of the cited works (Meta-MaxUp, DA-Fusion, MRAugment) or earlier diffusion-based augments realise simultaneously:
1) Class-specific semantic directions are discovered automatically by PCA on CLIP embeddings and projected into Stable-Diffusion latent space. DA-Fusion hand-crafts pseudo-prompts per class, and MRAugment & Meta-MaxUp stay in pixel space; none learn reusable latent axes without human vocabulary.
2) Augmentation magnitude is adjusted online from the classifier’s own entropy so the ‘difficulty schedule’ is closed-loop, whereas Meta-MaxUp uses loss maximisation once per batch and DA-Fusion uses a fixed random t0 schedule; no prior work ties diffusion edit strength to a live uncertainty signal.
3) Latent edit caching/replay amortises diffusion cost (<10 DDIM steps per mini-batch). Prior diffusion augmenters (DA-Fusion, AdaDiff) re-invert images every epoch and are ≥2× slower.
4) A tiny probe trained during training replaces static CLIP thresholds for label preservation, targeting the over/under-filtering problem unaddressed in previous methods.
5) The pieces are integrated into a lightweight Dataset wrapper that drops into any PyTorch pipeline, contrasting with the more intrusive training-loop changes required by Meta-MaxUp or MRAugment.
These innovations constitute a novel, closed-loop, semantics-aware augmentation framework rather than an incremental tweak on existing diffusion pipelines.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, SMART-Aug attacks two open problems—task-specific semantics and dynamic difficulty—demonstrating consistent gains (+2–4 pp on ImageNet-100 full data, +9 pp few-shot, −12 % mCE, +4 pp OOD AUROC) while reducing diffusion overhead by 15 % versus AdaDiff.  Robustness and calibration improvements indicate the method advances practical understanding of how model feedback can steer generative augmentations, likely spawning further work on closed-loop or RL-driven augmentation.
Societally, faster, more accurate classifiers with better OOD performance translate to safer deployment in domains like medical imaging (Camelyon17 results) and autonomous sensing.  Because SMART-Aug reuses edits and needs only 30 min one-off mining, it lowers compute cost and environmental footprint compared with prior diffusion augmenters.
Limitations (dependence on CLIP/SD availability, still 1.4× classic aug cost) temper but do not negate impact. Overall the method is a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-controllable data augmentation.

idea.open_problems:
Despite considerable progress, three pain-points remain for generative augmentation in everyday image classification.
P1 (adaptive semantics) Existing methods still assume that every class owns an independent set of latent edit directions. This ignores inter-class regularities (e.g. ‘background clutter’ is shared by birds & dogs) and wastes the one-off mining budget.
P2 (sample-wise difficulty) SMART-Aug uses entropy to set the edit magnitude, yet entropy alone conflates aleatoric noise (inherent image ambiguity) with epistemic weakness (knowledge gaps that augmentation could fix). Hence many edits are spent on already unlearnable samples.
P3 (cost & reproducibility) Even with an 8-step DDIM decode, diffusion remains ≥40 % of training time and prohibits training on commodity GPUs; furthermore, there is little understanding of how reproducible the mined directions are across datasets or backbones.
idea.methods:
We propose ReDi-Mix (REusable, DIfficulty-aware, MIXture augmentation), a drop-in PyTorch Dataset wrapper that tackles P1–P3 via three ideas.
Stage A : Hierarchical Semantic Mining (once per dataset)
A1 Collect CLIP embeddings for K images per class (K≈200).
A2 Perform supervised Contrastive Orthogonal Decomposition (COD): find d-vectors that simultaneously (i) maximise between-class variance and (ii) remain orthogonal to the class normal vector, thereby yielding directions that change *how* an object looks while keeping *what* it is. A stochastic Lanczos solver gives the top r global directions Dg and per-class residual directions Dc.
A3 Learn a light Mixture-of-Experts mapper M that predicts the mixing weights ω(x)∈R^{r} for any image embedding, s.t. SD-latent shift Σ_i ω_i d_i replicates the corresponding COD move. M is trained on 5 % of the images and generalises to unseen classes ⇒ mined directions become transferable.
Stage B : Cheap Mixed-latent Editing (every mini-batch)
B1 Encode an input image x→z.
B2 Sample β∈{0,1} deciding whether to use global or residual edits; choose d = Σ_i ω_i(x)·d_i if β=0 else d∈Dc.
B3 Magnitude m is drawn by a two-armed bandit that receives reward = −ℓ(x′) *1_{label preserved}. Thompson sampling quickly focuses on magnitudes that *reduce* loss for epistemically uncertain samples and ignores hopeless cases.
B4 Decode with 4 DDIM steps into a 64×64 preview; run the label-preservation probe on this thumbnail. Only accepted previews are up-scaled to full resolution with an extra 4 steps, cutting ≈60 % GPU time compared with unconditional 8-step decoding.
Stage C : Deterministic Re-Play
Latent deltas (d,m) and the preview are stored in a 512 MB RAM ring buffer. During later epochs the exact same delta is *added in feature space* after the first stage of the backbone (no diffusion) – a zero-cost, perfectly reproducible variant of the original edit.
Implementation is <500 lines, pure Python + PyTorch; no changes to optimiser or training loop.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
Among diffusion-based augmentation studies, prior work (e.g.
1) SMART-Aug – mines class-specific latent directions and sets edit strength by entropy,
2) DA-Fusion – steers Stable-Diffusion with text prompts or textual-inversion tokens per class, and

ReDi-Mix introduces three ideas that are absent from all cited works:

Neither SMART-Aug nor DA-Fusion share latent directions across classes or support cross-dataset re-use.
(2) A two-armed Thompson-sampling bandit that learns image-wise edit magnitude driven by loss improvement, thereby disentangling epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty; previous approaches rely on fixed schedules (DA-Fusion t0 range) or entropy proxies (SMART-Aug).
(3) A preview-then-replay pipeline that reduces diffusion to four 64×64 steps during mining and replaces later uses by deterministic feature-space deltas, achieving order-of-magnitude speed-ups and perfect reproducibility – a mechanism not explored in earlier diffusion augmentation papers.
Together these components allow edit directions to be mined *once* and replayed across models and datasets, which is a qualitatively new capability in the augmentation literature.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academic: ReDi-Mix demonstrates that a compact, shared pool of semantic directions combined with difficulty-aware magnitude control yields higher accuracy (+3–11 pp), better corruption robustness (mCE −10–15 %) and calibrated predictions while cutting diffusion cost by ≈60 %. It also provides the first empirical evidence that latent directions mined on one dataset can be transferred to another without re-running diffusion, challenging the prevailing belief that class- or dataset-specific editing is necessary.
Societal/engineering: By shrinking GPU time to only 1.2× RandAugment and enabling training on a single consumer GPU, the method lowers the compute and carbon barrier for practitioners who cannot afford large clusters. The replay buffer offers deterministic augmentation, aiding reproducibility – a pressing issue in ML. Finally, reusable edits open a path to building public "augmentation banks", potentially curbing the environmental footprint of diffusion models.
Limitations (e.g., dependence on CLIP embeddings, thumbnail-based label check) remain, but overall impact on both research methodology and practical accessibility is appreciable.
